content: Osgood-Schlatter disease, also referred to as tibial tubercle traumatic apophysitis or Louise's knees disease, is an inflammatory condition affecting the growth plate at the tibial tuberosity. It is classified as a type of osteochondritis. This condition is most frequently observed in active boys between the ages of 10 and 15. While it typically affects only one leg, it can occasionally occur in both legs simultaneously. The disease is named after Robert Bayley Osgood, an American surgeon, and Carl Schlatter, a Swiss surgeon, who were the first to describe it. In most cases, the condition resolves on its own over time. The primary cause of Osgood-Schlatter disease is repetitive stress on the patellar tendon, which connects the quadriceps muscle at the front of the thigh to the tibia. During an adolescent growth spurt, the stress from quadriceps contractions is transmitted through the patellar tendon to the tibial tuberosity, which is not yet fully developed. This can lead to inflammation, avulsion fractures, and subsequent bone growth within the tendon, resulting in a visible lump at the site. A characteristic symptom of this condition is the appearance of a visible bump, approximately 2 cm in diameter, at the tibial tubercle. This bump is often painful during and after high-impact activities, such as running or jumping, and sometimes even after less strenuous activities like climbing stairs. Although the disease is generally benign and self-limiting, symptoms can persist for 2 to 3 years. In most cases, the symptoms resolve by the end of the growth spurt or when the tibial epiphysis fuses. However, some adults may continue to experience pain when kneeling for the rest of their lives. Treatment for Osgood-Schlatter disease typically involves rest, application of ice, and stretching exercises. Analgesics may be used to alleviate pain. Physicians often recommend that patients temporarily refrain from physical activities that exacerbate the pain until symptoms subside. In cases where the condition persists, immobilization of the knee with a cast may be necessary. As a last resort, surgical intervention may be performed. This involves drilling multiple holes through the epiphyseal plate under anesthesia to promote fusion and alleviate the condition.
